speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) for each year between 2018 and 2022, what have been the Excess Wait Time (EWT) scores of (i) all buses operated by each public bus operator and (ii) service number 228; (b) whether the Public Transport Council took into account the EWT and On-Time Adherence scores of bus services when deciding on the 2.9% fare increase for the 2022 fare review exercise; and (c) if not, why not.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The fare formula, therefore, incorporates component indices, such as core inflation, wage growth and energy prices, which reflect the cost drivers of providing public transport services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The output of the fare formula establishes the fare increase cap for a given year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PTC then considers various other factors before deciding on the actual fare increase to implement and, consequently, how much to carry over to future Fare Review Exercises (FREs).

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PTC considers overall economic growth, wage growth, unemployment rate and other metrics that reflect the state of Singapore's economy at the time of each FRE.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PTC also seeks to ensure that public transport, as an essential service, remains affordable to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As wages have risen over the past decade, households have been spending a lower proportion of their income on public transport.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For the second decile of households, which essentially represents lower-income public transport users, this has fallen from 3.5% in 2012 to 2.5% in 2021.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For the second quintile, which represents average public transport users, that figure has also fallen from 2.3% to 1.8%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: One main contributory factor was the 117% increase in energy prices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This benefits all commuters as it defrays the overall fare increase.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To reiterate, without this additional support, commuters would have had to pay a much higher fare increase of 13.5%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At each FRE, PTC will also consider both the carry-over from previous FREs, as well as that year's fare formula output.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, for example, in 2021, the formula output was -2.2%, in other words, a reduction, but there was a carry-over amount of 4.4% and, therefore, the increase that was implemented was 2.2%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Apart from the 10.6% carried over from this year, all other carried-over amounts have been implemented.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Over the past decade, we have enhanced the quality of our public transport system, with a larger network, higher frequencies and more reliable services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Despite this, fares have not kept up with costs of running the public transport system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: From 2012 to 2021, the compounded increase in costs has been about 7%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Fares have been increasing over the same period at about 1% a year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the Government has stepped up with funding to bridge the gap and ensure the continued operation of public transport services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The cumulative sum is now more than $2 billion a year, with the additional subsidy of about $200 million in the coming year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Gerald Giam has asked whether PTC decides on fare adjustments based on bus service reliability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have made steady improvements over the past decade, with maximum scheduled frequencies during peak periods falling from 30 minutes to 15 minutes today.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of Excess Wait Time (EWT) and On-Time Adherence (OTA) scores between 2018 and 2022, all services have met the required standards, and this includes service 228, which, I know, is close to Mr Gerald Giam's heart.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Looking ahead, it is essential that public transport fares keep pace with cost increases.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Otherwise, the public transport system will become financially unsustainable and that will be to the detriment of commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When PTC reviews fares, it will continue to ensure that any increases are subject to prevailing economic and social considerations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, let me reassure Members that we are fully committed to ensuring that public transport fares remain affordable, even as we keep a keen eye on the financial sustainability of our public transport system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, seniors, students, lower-wage workers and persons with disabilities are eligible for concession fares and increases in their fares are typically less than that for adult commuters.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government has also made available Public Transport Vouchers (PTVs) to cushion the impact of fare increases for eligible households.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For this year's FRE, these vouchers will help up to the 30th percentile of income-earning households, or the 40th percentile of all resident households.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we will continue to address the needs of vulnerable commuters through the provision of PTVs and other measures as necessary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, bus service 228 is very close to my heart and, more importantly, close to the hearts of my residents in Bedok Reservoir.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What is really the interval, because I just checked the bus stop opposite Block 716 in Bedok Reservoir Road and it shows an interval of seven to 15 minutes, which I would think that it is a bit long because, previously, residents had several other buses to be able to get to Bedok Interchange from their houses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, they depend on that bus and the low interval of that bus.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I note that his questions are very specific, and actually quite a deviation from public transport fares themselves.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think it is very hard to give a universally applicable answer.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The reason is because the same bus service, or the time of day, there will be variations because of traffic conditions, such as peak, off-peak.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Peak periods, you try to keep the headway shorter because of the needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there will always be a range and that also applies to geographic distribution.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are incentives and disincentives that apply when they deviate.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, of course, if the deviations are systematic or problematic, then we take further action in that regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Well, this is basically re-canvassing the discussions we have had at the Budget and many other occasions, and I compliment the Member on his consistency in raising the issue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the bottom line is this: every decision has an accompanying cost implication.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I notice the Member has not commented on the 2.9% increase.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I assume the Member finds it acceptable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But bear in mind that this comes with a significant subsidy from the Government, on top of what we are already doing for this year.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Every time we reduce headways, it means you either have to have more buses and, therefore, you also need more bus captains, costs will go up and we have to find ways to address this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is not a theoretical argument either, because over the years, if you look at it, in terms of rail reliability – mean kilometres between failures – we have actually made significant improvements because the Land Transport Authority (LTA) has specified an outcome.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: To achieve that number or exceed it, then the PTOs have to invest significant resources on maintenance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have added, I think, about 80-odd new bus services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, when we advocate, sure, I think we would all like to have shorter headways, more capacity and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I just want to make the point that even as we consider this, we also have to take into account the cost implications and, as this year's exercise demonstrates, there is a major cost overhang that we are carrying, and we are carrying this as a Government, as representatives of the people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The supplementary question I am going to ask is in relation to the gap that the Minister mentioned.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a 7% increase in the cost of transport expenditure and infrastructure itself, as the Minister mentioned before.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also just now, the Minister mentioned about the 1% transport price increase annually.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, there is this gap of about 6%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whether this gap is sustainable is one question that I have, and will the Government subsidies eventually stop?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The second supplementary question is in relation to the PTVs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can I ask if, eventually, these PTVs can be permanent or enhanced even further and made automatic in future Budgets?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But let me address the questions very quickly with your indulgence, Sir.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think we will need to take a hard look at this and that is what the PTC is working on – what exactly is the way forward for us.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is not just about the sums, but it really comes down to an overall discussion on the compact that we expect.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And fare formula and fare adjustments are not just about the current generation because everything we do not pay now, as we discussed in other debates, also has an impact on future generations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we need to keep that in mind.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we do going forward, will again, be a matter of discussion that we will have to also address in this House as part of our larger policy with respect to public transport.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I suspect that question is best addressed by the Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I would argue that from our perspective – and I want to reiterate the point – we are committed to making sure fares are affordable, especially for vulnerable commuters.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That includes not just in the way we address fare increase adjustments and the discounts for what we can do and, also through the concession passes, but it is also through PTVs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think that is a major provision and we will continue to see what else needs to be done in that regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I suppose permanent PTVs could be one of the possibilities, but I think that we should just see through this exercise first.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, there is indeed a cost to everything.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The tea break today is 17 minutes, instead of 20 minutes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: [Pursuant to Standing Order No 22(3), provided that Members had not asked for questions standing in their names to be postponed to a later Sitting day or withdrawn, written answers to questions not reached by the end of Question Time are reproduced in the Appendix.]
